title: Sultanate of Rum
subtitle: 1071–1308 · Konya, the Caravanserais, Myriokephalon and the Mongol Protectorate

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Suleyman at Nicaea, Konya's sultans from Masud to Kayqubad, the Mongol vassals and the last princes of the line

entries.label: Suleyman ibn Qutalmish at Nicaea
entries.hint: Suleyman, a Seljuk prince and a cousin of the Great Seljuk sultan, took Nicaea in the civil wars of the Byzantine empire and made it a capital for a Turkish state in Anatolia, where his Turkmen warriors served as the allies of Byzantine pretenders. He was killed in 1086 fighting the Great Seljuk governor of Syria near Aleppo.
entries.note: Anna Komnene, Alexiad 3.11; Ibn al-Athir; Claude Cahen, Pre-Ottoman Turkey (1968); Beihammer 2017.

entries.label: Kilij Arslan I
entries.hint: Kilij Arslan, Suleyman's son, took the throne after years in captivity at the Great Seljuk court. He lost Nicaea to the First Crusade in 1097, destroyed the three crusading armies of 1101 in the plateau, and drowned in the Khabur in 1107 in a fight for Mosul. His state, thrown back onto the plateau, took Konya as its base, and his successors made it the capital.
entries.note: Anna Komnene 6, 11; Albert of Aachen; Ibn al-Athir; Cahen 1968.

entries.label: Masud I and Kilij Arslan II
entries.hint: Masud I made Konya his capital, defeated Conrad III's crusaders at Dorylaeum in 1147 and began the mosque of Alaeddin. His grandson Kilij Arslan II ruled for 36 years, humbled Manuel Komnenos at Myriokephalon in 1176, destroyed his Danishmendid rivals and made Konya the leading city of the plateau. In 1186 he divided his lands among his sons.
entries.note: Niketas Choniates, Historia; John Kinnamos; Ibn Bibi; Cahen 1968; Speros Vryonis, The Decline of Medieval Hellenism in Asia Minor (1971).

entries.label: Kaykhusraw I
entries.hint: Kaykhusraw, the youngest son of Kilij Arslan II, was driven out in 1196 by his brothers and spent years as the guest of the Byzantine emperor, who adopted him as a son. He took Konya back in 1205, captured the port of Antalya in 1207 and was killed in 1211 in a battle against the Nicaean emperor Theodore Laskaris at Alaşehir.
entries.note: Niketas Choniates; Ibn Bibi; George Akropolites; Cahen 1968.

entries.label: Kayqubad I — the golden age
entries.hint: Alaeddin Kayqubad took Alanya in 1221, rebuilt the walls of Konya, built caravanserais across the plateau and the palace of Kubadabad on Lake Beyşehir, and beat the Khwarazmian Jalal al-Din at Yassıçemen in 1230. Under him the sultanate reached its greatest wealth, a court of Persian poets and scholars with the Mongols still far off.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi, al-Awamir al-Ala'iyya; Ibn Bibi's Persian chronicle; Cahen 1968; Scott Redford on Kubadabad.

entries.label: Kaykhusraw II
entries.hint: Kaykhusraw II, Kayqubad's son, ruled under the power of his vizier Sa'd al-Din Köpek until he had him killed in 1239. A great revolt of the Turkmen, the Babai rising of 1240, shook the state and in 1243 the Mongol army under Baiju crushed him at Köse Dağ. He became a vassal of the Great Khan.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Bar Hebraeus, Chronography; Cahen 1968.

entries.label: The sons and the Pervane
entries.hint: Kaykhusraw II's three sons, Kaykaus II, Kilij Arslan IV and Kayqubad II, were set up as joint sultans under Mongol supervision and fought one another until Kilij Arslan IV was made sole sultan in 1260. The real ruler from 1261 to 1277 was the Pervane Mu'in al-Din Suleyman, a vizier who played the Ilkhans against the Mamluks and was executed by the Ilkhan Abaqa.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Aksarayi, Musamarat al-akhbar; Cahen 1968; Peter Jackson, The Mongols and the West (2005).

entries.label: Masud II and the end of the line
entries.hint: Masud II and Kayqubad III were puppets of the Ilkhans, set on and off the throne between 1282 and 1308. When Masud II died in 1308, the Ilkhan Oljeitu did not appoint a successor, and the sultanate came to an end in the hands of a Mongol governor. The family's name was kept by the Turkmen principalities that took its place.
entries.note: Aksarayi, Musamarat al-akhbar; Anonymous Seljuk Chronicle; Cahen 1968.

entries.label: The Danishmendids and the other Turkmen dynasties
entries.hint: In the northeast and east of Anatolia, rival Turkmen dynasties held their own: the Danishmendids at Sivas and Malatya, the Mengujekids at Erzincan and Divriği, the Saltukids at Erzurum. They fought each other, the Byzantines and the crusaders, and were absorbed one by one by the Seljuks of Rum by 1178.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Michael the Syrian; Cahen 1968; Irene Beldiceanu-Steinherr on the Danishmendids.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Turkmen conquest, the crusades across the plateau, Myriokephalon, Köse Dağ, the Babai revolt and Baybars at Elbistan

entries.label: The Turkmen conquest of the plateau
entries.hint: After Manzikert and the civil wars of the Byzantines, bands of Turkmen under chiefs of their own took the plateau with little resistance, settled in the plains and the high pastures and besieged cities. By 1081 they held the whole of central Anatolia to Nicaea and Cyzicus. The collapse owed more to Byzantine civil wars than to the Turks' strength.
entries.note: Nikephoros Bryennios, Material for History; Attaleiates; Anna Komnene 1–3; Beihammer 2017.

entries.label: Nicaea and Dorylaeum
entries.hint: The First Crusade, with Byzantine help, took Nicaea in June 1097 and defeated Kilij Arslan's army at Dorylaeum on 1 July. The Turks were driven from the west of the plateau and the Byzantines retook the Aegean coast. Kilij Arslan's capital was lost and the sultanate moved to Konya.
entries.note: Gesta Francorum 1–9; Anna Komnene 11; Albert of Aachen; Steven Runciman, A History of the Crusades vol. 1.

entries.label: The crusade of 1101
entries.hint: Three new crusading armies, from Lombardy, from Nevers and from Aquitaine and Bavaria, crossed Anatolia in 1101 and were destroyed one by one by Kilij Arslan and the Danishmendids at Mersivan (Merzifon) and Heraclea (Ereğli). Few reached Syria. The defeat taught the Franks to keep to the coast.
entries.note: Albert of Aachen 8; Ekkehard of Aura; Ibn al-Athir; Runciman vol. 2.

entries.label: Dorylaeum 1147
entries.hint: Masud I's cavalry fell on Conrad III's German crusaders on the march across Anatolia in the Second Crusade, in October 1147, destroying most of the army near Dorylaeum. Louis VII's French crusaders were cut about at the Meander in the following winter. The Second Crusade, in Anatolia, was a failure.
entries.note: Odo of Deuil; Otto of Freising, Gesta Friderici; Niketas Choniates; Runciman vol. 2.

entries.label: Myriokephalon
entries.hint: Manuel I Komnenos led his army into a mountain pass on the way to Konya and was ambushed by Kilij Arslan II's cavalry at Myriokephalon. His losses were heavy, though the army was not destroyed. He made terms that included the destruction of the fortresses of Dorylaeum and Sublaeum. It ended the Komnenian reconquest of Anatolia.
entries.note: Niketas Choniates, Historia 4.8; John Kinnamos 7; Paul Magdalino, The Empire of Manuel I Komnenos (1993).

entries.label: Barbarossa at Iconium
entries.hint: Frederick Barbarossa's army, on the Third Crusade, crossed Anatolia in May 1190 over the opposition of the sultan's son Qutb al-Din, defeated the Turks in front of Konya and took the city. The emperor drowned in the Göksu river soon after, and the army dissolved. The Seljuks were not displaced.
entries.note: Historia de expeditione Friderici imperatoris; Ansbert; Ibn al-Athir; Cahen 1968.

entries.label: The ports on both seas
entries.hint: Kaykhusraw I took Antalya in 1207, Kaykaus I took Sinop from the Greek emperor of Trebizond in 1214 and Kayqubad I took Alanya in 1221. With ports on the Mediterranean and the Black Sea the sultanate had access to world trade. Antalya was held by the Seljuks for the next century.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; George Akropolites; Cahen 1968.

entries.label: The Babai revolt
entries.hint: A Turkmen dervish, Baba Ishak, called by his followers Baba Rasul Allah, preached an end to the sultan's government and led a rising of Turkmen and peasants that spread from Amasya to Sivas and Malatya in 1240. The sultan's army, with Frankish mercenaries, defeated it at Kırşehir with heavy losses.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Bar Hebraeus; Aflaki; Ahmet Yaşar Ocak on the Babai revolt.

entries.label: Köse Dağ
entries.hint: The Mongol general Baiju, with Georgians and Armenians, met Kaykhusraw II's much larger army, of Turkmen, Georgians, Franks and Greeks, in the Köse Dağ near Erzincan, and in one day destroyed it. The sultan fled and the Mongol army took Sivas and Kayseri. The sultanate paid a tribute and became a vassal.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Bar Hebraeus; Het'um of Korykos; Jackson 2005.

entries.label: Baybars at Elbistan
entries.hint: Invited by a Turkmen faction led by the Karamanid Mehmed Bey, the Mamluk sultan Baybars marched into Anatolia and defeated the Mongol army at Elbistan in April 1277, then entered Kayseri. When he withdrew, the Ilkhan Abaqa came to punish the land.
entries.note: Ibn Shaddad; Aksarayi; al-Maqrizi; Reuven Amitai-Preiss, Mongols and Mamluks (1995).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The sultan's court, the Persian chancery, the iqta, the akhis and the Mongol tribute

entries.label: The court and the iqta
entries.hint: The sultanate was ruled by a court of amirs, with a vizier, a chancery in Persian, an atabeg for the princes and a military aristocracy supported by iqta grants of revenue and the pastoral Turkmen at the frontier. The model was that of the Great Seljuks, simplified. The sultan's household was of Greek, Georgian and Armenian wives and slave-soldiers.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Cahen 1968; Ann Lambton on the iqta; Rudi Lindner, Nomads and Ottomans in Medieval Anatolia (1983).

entries.label: Persian as the language of state
entries.hint: The sultan's chancery, history and poetry were in Persian, the court tongue of the whole eastern Seljuk world, while Arabic was the language of religion and Turkish that of the soldiers. The sultanate was called Rum, 'the Roman land', by its neighbours, and its rulers took the Persian royal names Kaykhusraw and Kayqubad.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Aksarayi; Cahen 1968; Andrew Peacock on Seljuk Persian culture.

entries.label: The akhi brotherhoods
entries.hint: In the towns of the plateau the akhis, a brotherhood of artisans and young men organised along the lines of the Islamic futuwwa, with a code of generosity and hospitality, kept order, defended the town and built their guild hostels (zawiya). Akhi Evran, the patron saint of the tanners, lived in Kırşehir.
entries.note: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (on the akhis, 1330s); Franz Taeschner, Gülschehris Mesnevi (1932); Cahen 1968.

entries.label: The Mongol tribute and census
entries.hint: After Köse Dağ the sultanate was made to pay an annual tribute in gold, horses and cloth, and in the 1250s a Mongol census and tax assessment was made. The burden fell on the peasantry and the towns, and on the Seljuk treasury, which debased the dirham.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Bar Hebraeus; Jackson 2005; Cahen 1968.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Rumi and the Mevlevis, Hacı Bektaş, Ibn Arabi's circle and the Christians under the sultans

entries.label: Christians under the sultans
entries.hint: Greek and Armenian Christians stayed as peasants and townspeople, in Cappadocia in particular, with their bishops and monasteries, and the metropolitan of Iconium continued in the Greek church. The sultans married Christian princesses and took their advice, and rock-churches were still painted in Cappadocia in the 1200s. The Islamisation of the plateau was slow.
entries.note: Speros Vryonis, The Decline of Medieval Hellenism (1971); Aflaki; Ibn Bibi; Lyn Rodley on Cappadocian churches.

entries.label: Ibn Arabi and Qunawi in Anatolia
entries.hint: The great Andalusian mystic Ibn Arabi spent years at Konya, Malatya and Sivas in the first third of the thirteenth century, and made a disciple and son-in-law of Sadr al-Din Qunawi, who taught his thought in Konya for forty years and was a friend of Rumi. The Akbarian school spread through Anatolia and Persia.
entries.note: Ibn Arabi, Futuhat al-Makkiyya; William Chittick, The Self-Disclosure of God (1998); Qunawi, Miftah al-ghayb.

entries.label: Rumi and the Mevlevis
entries.hint: Jalal al-Din Rumi came as a boy with his father from Balkh and settled in Konya, where he was a teacher of religious law until the dervish Shams of Tabriz appeared in 1244 and changed his life. He wrote the Masnavi, a poem of some 25,000 couplets on the soul's return to God, and thousands of lyrics. After his death in 1273 his son founded the Mevlevi order.
entries.note: Rumi, Masnavi and Divan-i Shams; Aflaki, Manaqib al-arifin (c. 1318); Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present (2000).

entries.label: Hacı Bektaş and the Anatolian dervishes
entries.hint: Hacı Bektaş, a Khurasani dervish who settled in central Anatolia after the Babai revolt, became the patron saint of the Bektashi order, which mingled Sufi, Shia and older Turkmen traditions and had a great following among the Turkmen and later the Janissaries. Little is known of his life; the Vilayetname tells his legend.
entries.note: Vilayetname of Hacı Bektaş (15th c.); Irène Mélikoff, Hadji Bektach (1998).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Alaeddin mosque, Divriği, Kubadabad's tiles, Yunus Emre and the music of the reed

entries.label: The Alaeddin Mosque of Konya
entries.hint: Begun under Masud I and completed under Kayqubad I, the Alaeddin Mosque, on the citadel hill, has a forest of columns, many reused from Byzantine ruins, carrying a flat roof, and a dome of brick, with a magnificent carved wooden minbar. The Ince Minare Madrasa (1264) has a famous carved portal. The mosque held the tombs of the sultans.
entries.note: Inscriptions of the Alaeddin Mosque; Gönül Öney, Anadolu Selçuklu Mimarisinde Süsleme (1978); Scott Redford.

entries.label: The tiles of Kubadabad
entries.hint: The summer palace of Kayqubad I on the shore of Lake Beyşehir was decorated with underglaze-painted and lustre tiles in the shape of stars and crosses, with figures of animals, birds, courtiers and fantastic creatures. Excavations since the 1960s have recovered many hundreds. The tiles show a world of palace life in the sultan's own image.
entries.note: Katharina Otto-Dorn and Mehmet Önder, Kubad-Abad (1966–); Rüçhan Arık, Kubad-Abad (2000).

entries.label: The Great Mosque and Hospital of Divriği
entries.hint: Ahmad Shah, Mengujekid ruler of Divriği, built a mosque and a hospital, side by side, by the architect Khurram Shah of Akhlat. Their portals are covered in some of the most exuberant carved stone decoration of the Islamic world. They were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985.
entries.note: Founders' inscriptions; Gönül Öney 1978; UNESCO World Heritage List no. 358.

entries.label: The reed and the sema
entries.hint: The Masnavi begins with the lament of the reed flute torn from its reed bed, and the Mevlevi dervishes, with Rumi and his son Sultan Veled, developed a ritual of whirling dance to the music of the ney (reed), the kudüm drums and the voice. The sema, now recognised by UNESCO, was fixed in the generation after Rumi.
entries.note: Rumi, Masnavi 1.1–18; Sultan Veled, Ibtida-nama; Aflaki; UNESCO Intangible Heritage (Mevlevi Sema, 2008).

entries.label: Yunus Emre and the Turkish poem
entries.hint: Yunus Emre, a village mystic of Anatolia, wrote in the language of the people, in simple Turkish syllabic verse about love, God and the oneness of creation, at a time when courtly poetry was in Persian. His poems, handed down orally and in manuscripts, are the beginning of a Turkish literary tradition in Anatolia.
entries.note: Yunus Emre, Divan; Risalat al-nushiyya; Talat Tekin, Yunus Emre (1971).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Ibn Bibi, Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, the school of medicine at Kayseri and Qunawi

entries.label: The Gevher Nesibe medical school
entries.hint: In Kayseri, in 1205–1206, a hospital and a medical school with twin domes and a courtyard were built in memory of Gevher Nesibe, daughter of Kilij Arslan II. The founding charter provides for physicians, students, and the feeding of the sick. It is the oldest medical school of the Turks in Anatolia.
entries.note: Waqf and building inscriptions of the Gevher Nesibe complex; Cahen 1968; Gönül Öney.

entries.label: Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi
entries.hint: Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, pupil of Nasir al-Din Tusi at Maragha, came to Anatolia, served as a judge at Sivas and Malatya and wrote in Konya and elsewhere on astronomy, medicine and philosophy. His model of planetary motion, an alternative to Ptolemy's, built on Tusi's work and is part of the tradition in Maragha that influenced Copernicus.
entries.note: Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, Nihayat al-idrak; Tuhfa shahiyya; George Saliba, A History of Arabic Astronomy (1994).

entries.label: Ibn Bibi's Persian chronicle
entries.hint: Ibn Bibi, a chancery official of Persian origin, wrote in high Persian, at the request of the Ilkhanid vizier, a history of the Seljuks of Rum from 1192 to 1280 — the Royal Commands, in ornate prose with verse. It is the main source on the sultanate and a monument of Persian court style.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi, al-Awamir al-ala'iyya fi'l-umur al-ala'iyya (ed. Zhukovsky); H. W. Duda, Die Seltschukengeschichte des Ibn Bibi (1959).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The caravan trade, the ports on the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, the carpets of Turcomania and the Mongol levy

entries.label: The Turkmen and the pastures
entries.hint: The Turkmen, who came with their flocks of sheep and horses in search of summer pastures, turned the plateau, with its steppe and mountain meadows, into a land of herds. They moved between winter quarters (kışlak) and summer pastures (yaylak) and lived beside the farming villages. The prosperity of the sultanate rested on both.
entries.note: Rudi Lindner 1983; Cahen 1968; Vryonis 1971.

entries.label: The ports and the caravan trade
entries.hint: After the sultans took the ports, a trade grew in Anatolian goods — carpets, alum, copper, horses, hides, slaves — and Mediterranean commerce reached the interior through Antalya and Alanya and the Black Sea through Sinop and Samsun. Cypriot, Venetian and Genoese merchants came to the ports, and treaties set the tolls. The trade was a state interest.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Cahen 1968; Michel Balard on the Italian trade; Marco Polo, Travels.

entries.label: The carpets of Turcomania
entries.hint: Wool pile carpets of the thirteenth century, with large geometric patterns and borders, were found in the Alaeddin Mosque of Konya and the Eşrefoğlu Mosque at Beyşehir. Marco Polo wrote that the best and handsomest carpets in the world were made in Turcomania. They are the oldest large group of surviving carpets in the world.
entries.note: Alaeddin Mosque carpets (Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts, Istanbul; Mevlana Museum); Marco Polo, Travels 1.1.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: A network of caravanserais, the shipyard of Alanya and the tile

entries.label: The network of caravanserais
entries.hint: The sultans and their viziers built a system of fortified inns of stone on the main roads, a day's march apart, with a great portal, a courtyard, an open and a covered hall and a small mosque. Sultan Han at Aksaray (1229) and near Kayseri (1232–36) are the finest. Some hundred were built, and travellers were housed free for three days.
entries.note: Inscriptions of the hans; Kurt Erdmann, Das anatolische Karavansaray (1961–76); Cahen 1968.

entries.label: The tile
entries.hint: Seljuk masters developed mosaic tilework of cut turquoise, blue and black glazed pieces for mihrabs and domes, at the Karatay Madrasa and the Sırçalı Madrasa, and underglaze-painted tiles, and the moulded glazed brick. The brilliant blue of the Seljuk tile became a mark of Anatolian architecture.
entries.note: Karatay Madrasa (1251–52); Sırçalı Madrasa (1242); Gönül Öney 1978.

entries.label: Alanya's walls and dockyard
entries.hint: After taking Alanya (Kalonoros) in 1221, Kayqubad built a great fortress on the peninsula with walls of nearly seven kilometres, the Kızıl Kule, a hexagonal tower of 1226, by a Syrian architect, and a covered shipyard of 1228 with five aisles for building galleys. The port city was the sultan's winter home.
entries.note: Founders' inscriptions of Alanya (Red Tower, 1226; shipyard, 1228); Ibn Bibi.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Kilij Arslan's visit to Manuel, Marco Polo on the road, refugees from the Mongols and the treaty with Trebizond

entries.label: Kilij Arslan II visits Constantinople
entries.hint: In 1161 the sultan went in person to Constantinople, accepted a peace and a kind of vassalage to Manuel I, and was entertained with horse races, banquets and a hunt, receiving gifts and the promise of an annual subsidy. The visit made him the emperor's 'son', and gave him a freer hand against the Danishmendids.
entries.note: John Kinnamos 5.4–5; Niketas Choniates 3.2; Magdalino 1993.

entries.label: The treaty with Trebizond
entries.hint: After Sinop fell to Kaykaus I in 1214 and its Greek ruler was captured, the empire of Trebizond became a tributary of the sultan and paid him a tribute. Its emperor Alexios I was said to have served in the Seljuk campaigns. Trebizond was a Black Sea vassal of Konya until the Mongols.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Michael Panaretos; Anthony Bryer, The Empire of Trebizond and the Pontos (1980).

entries.label: The refugees from the Mongols
entries.hint: As the Mongols overran Khurasan and Iran, scholars, mystics, poets and craftsmen fled west to Konya, where the sultans gave them honour. Baha al-Din Walad, Rumi's father, and his family, Ibn Arabi, Najm al-Din Dayeh and many Persian courtiers came. The sultanate drew in a part of Iran's learning.
entries.note: Aflaki; Ibn Bibi; Cahen 1968.

entries.label: Marco Polo in Turcomania
entries.hint: On his way to China, Marco Polo passed through the Mongol-ruled Anatolia and described its three peoples, the Turkmen, Armenians and Greeks, and its trade: carpets, silks, horses and mules, and the cities of Konya, Kayseri and Sivas. He gives the Anatolian trade a place on the Silk Road.
entries.note: Marco Polo, Travels 1.1.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Turkification of Anatolia, the Fourth Crusade's aftermath and the Mongol conquest

entries.label: The Turkification of Anatolia
entries.hint: Over two centuries the Turkmen immigration, the withdrawal of the Byzantine administration and the conversion of Christian peasants changed the plateau from a Greek and Armenian land to a Turkish-speaking Muslim one, a process that is still debated in its speed and in how much replacement it involved and how much conversion. By 1300 the plateau's peoples were of mixed descent.
entries.note: Speros Vryonis 1971; Cahen 1968; Beihammer 2017; Sergei Karpov on interpretations.

entries.label: The Fourth Crusade and the Greek exiles
entries.hint: The Latin conquest of Constantinople in 1204 left three Greek states in Asia: the empire of Nicaea under Theodore Laskaris, the empire of Trebizond under the Komnenoi and a Greek state in the west. The sultan used the quarrels to take the Mediterranean coast and the road to the Black Sea.
entries.note: Niketas Choniates; George Akropolites; Michael Angold, A Byzantine Government in Exile (1975).

entries.label: The Mongol conquest of Anatolia
entries.hint: After Köse Dağ the Mongols made Anatolia a province of their empire, with garrisons in the eastern plains and the sultans as puppets. They turned the plateau into a theatre of Mongol and Mamluk rivalry, which ended Seljuk independence and encouraged the independent power of the Turkmen on the frontiers.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Jackson 2005; Charles Melville on the Mongols in Anatolia.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Mahperi Hatun, Gurju Khatun, the vizier Köpek and the women round Rumi

entries.label: Mahperi Hatun
entries.hint: Mahperi Huand Hatun, a wife of Kayqubad I of Greek or Christian origin and the mother of Kaykhusraw II, built in Kayseri a great complex of mosque, madrasa, bath and tomb, in 1237–1238, of which the Huand Hatun mosque remains. She was one of the great female patrons of Anatolia in the Middle Ages and a regent for a time.
entries.note: Inscriptions of the Huand Hatun complex (Kayseri); Ibn Bibi; Cahen 1968.

entries.label: Women round Rumi
entries.hint: Hagiographers of the Mevlevi order tell of Rumi's wife Gawhar Khatun and Kerra Khatun, of Fakhr al-Nisa and others who were his disciples, and of women who took part in the sema. The stories are late and idealised, but women had a place in the Sufi circles of Konya.
entries.note: Aflaki, Manaqib al-arifin; Franklin Lewis 2000.

entries.label: Sa'd al-Din Köpek
entries.hint: Köpek, a slave-born amir who became the vizier of Kaykhusraw II, used his power to purge the Seljuk court of the old amirs and princes, with tortures and killings, until in 1239 he was himself seized and executed. The story shows the dangers of the slave-soldier system.
entries.note: Ibn Bibi; Bar Hebraeus; Cahen 1968.

entries.label: Gurju Khatun
entries.hint: Gurju Khatun, a Georgian princess who married Kaykhusraw II and later the Pervane, was a friend and patron of Rumi and had great influence at the court of the Mongol vassals. She was among Rumi's patrons and had a great part in the court's affairs. Her importance shows the role of Christian-born women at the court.
entries.note: Aflaki, Manaqib al-arifin; Ibn Bibi; Lewis 2000.
